title: Missing
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 25 of 40
content:
Maxson gave the order without raising his voice.

That made it worse.

Paladin Danse was a synth. A security threat. An abomination created by the Institute. His service record did not matter. His loyalty did not matter. His years in the Brotherhood did not matter.

Find him.

Execute him.

Return with his holotags.

I stood in the command deck listening to the machinery of Danse’s worldview turn against him.

“Was there evidence he knew?” I asked.

Maxson’s eyes hardened.

“That is irrelevant.”

“It is extremely relevant.”

“He is a synth.”

“He is Danse.”

“That name belongs to a lie.”

Anger came up so fast I tasted metal.

“He bled for you.”

“So have thousands.”

“He led your people. He recovered your technology. He lost half his squad carrying out Brotherhood orders.”

“And if the Institute planted him to do exactly that?”

That stopped me.

Not because I believed it.

Because fear was persuasive when it wore uncertainty.

Maxson saw the hesitation.

“That is why the order stands.”

I left before I said something that would get me shot.

Haylen was waiting near the flight deck.

She had packed supplies into my bag.

“RadAway. Stimpaks. Fusion cells. Food.”

I took it.

“You’re helping me disobey a direct order.”

“I’m helping you complete a mission.”

“Haylen.”

Her mouth trembled.

“Bring him back if you can.”

I did not promise.

Promises felt dangerous.

Listening Post Bravo sat hidden beneath a ruined structure north of the city. I traveled alone because nobody else could know where I was going.

The Commonwealth seemed determined to slow me down.

Rain began by noon. Mirelurks forced me off the river road. A pack of ferals trapped me inside a laundromat for forty minutes.

Every delay fed the same thought.

What if Danse obeyed before I got there?

He had told me what Brotherhood protocol meant.

He had told me about Cutler.

He had said dangerous things did not become safe because they were familiar.

Would he apply that logic to himself?

Of course he would.

That terrified me more than Maxson’s order.

I reached the listening post after dark.

The entrance was concealed behind a security door half buried in concrete.

Danse’s access code still worked.

The elevator descended too slowly.

I could hear my own breathing.

The doors opened onto a narrow bunker corridor lit by red emergency lamps.

“Danse?”

No answer.

I moved deeper.

A Brotherhood holotag lay on a table.

His.

My stomach turned.

Then a voice came from the room beyond.

“You shouldn’t have come.”

I closed my eyes.

Alive.

I stepped through the doorway.

Danse sat on a cot wearing his Brotherhood uniform without armor. His rifle leaned against the wall out of reach.

He looked terrible.

Not injured.

Worse.

Empty.

I crossed the room before I remembered to be careful.

He stood.

“Stop.”

I stopped.

His eyes were red-rimmed from exhaustion.

“How did you find me?”

“Haylen.”

He looked away.

“I told her not to interfere.”

“She ignored an order. Terrible influence.”

Usually that would have earned something.

Nothing.

Danse looked at the holotag on the table.

“Maxson sent you.”

It was not a question.

“Yes.”

His face tightened.

“To execute me.”

“Yes.”

The word tore on the way out.

Danse nodded.

“Then do it.”

Everything inside me stopped.

“No.”

His expression hardened.

“You have your orders.”

“I said no.”

“You swore an oath.”

“I don’t care.”

“I do.”

His voice cracked through the bunker.

I stared at him.

He was shaking.

Not visibly enough that anyone else might notice.

I knew him now.

“I’m a synth,” he said. “The exact thing we’ve been fighting.”

“You’re Danse.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is to me.”

His face twisted.

“You don’t understand.”

“I understand Maxson wants me to kill the man I—”

I stopped.

Love hovered there.

Neither of us was ready for it.

Danse heard it anyway.

His eyes closed.

“Don’t,” he whispered.

The bunker suddenly felt like ArcJet again.

Danse standing beneath a machine, ordering me to press the button.

Only this time there would be no power armor.

And I had learned something since then.

Following an order did not make the consequence easier to live with.

I took one step closer.

“No,” I said again. “Not this time.”

The road to Bravo took me past places Danse and I had crossed together.

That made the journey crueler.

The ruined service station where he had first admitted he was tired.

The bridge where we argued about Amos.

A stretch of road where he had once corrected my spacing three times in five minutes.

Now there was no armored shape six feet off my left side.

I hated the empty space.

Near dusk I found fresh laser burns on the shell of an old car.

Brotherhood pattern.

My stomach dropped.

I crouched beside the road and studied the marks.

One attacker. Maybe two. The shots had come from the west. Return fire had struck a concrete barrier at shoulder height.

Danse had been here.

I knew his shooting the way I knew his footsteps by then: controlled pairs, center mass, no wasted sweep.

A dead raider lay behind the barrier with a laser burn through the chest.

Alive, then.

Alive recently.

I stood too quickly and had to steady myself against the car.

“Get a grip.”

The words sounded like him.

That helped more than I wanted to admit.

I kept moving.

At the next ridge a Brotherhood vertibird crossed far to the south.

I dropped beneath a concrete overhang and watched it pass.

For months, that sound had meant Danse’s people.

Now it meant danger.

I wondered what it felt like for him to hear it.

The thought turned my stomach again.

By full dark I had reached the ruined structure above Bravo.

Before entering, I sat on the broken steps and forced myself to eat half a ration bar.

Danse would have told me I was useless if I arrived dehydrated and shaking.

Actually, he would have said *operationally compromised.*

I drank water too.

Then I took the holotag he had once handed me during power armor training—the spare tag he used to demonstrate how Brotherhood identification codes were stamped.

I had kept it as a joke.

The metal felt heavy now.

What makes a person?

A number on a tag?

A number in an Institute registry?

A body grown instead of born?

A memory that might have happened to someone else?

None of the answers I had pushed Danse toward seemed clean enough when the question wore his face.

I was afraid.

Not only that he might be dead.

That he might be dangerous.

Maxson’s argument had lodged where I hated it most. What if there was a command hidden inside him? What if the Institute had built his loyalty as camouflage? What if love made me stupid?

I let the fears exist.

Then I asked myself one simpler question.

What had Danse chosen when nobody was forcing him?

He had stopped for civilians.

He had buried his dead.

He had helped Amos after insulting him.

He had saved Nick before his doctrine could object.

He had filed a report to keep water running because he decided an order could wait.

He had held my hand in thunderstorms and pretended it was logistics.

Those choices were evidence too.

Not proof of safety.

Proof of personhood.

I stood.

The closer I got to Bravo, the more Maxson’s words tried to become Danse’s voice in my head.

Machine. Infiltrator. Threat.

Then another memory answered.

Danse at ArcJet, ordering me out of the engine chamber before the test fired.

Danse carrying Haylen through dust after the floor collapse.

Danse standing between Amos and a raider bullet before his prejudice had time to approve.

None of those memories proved he was incapable of danger.

People were dangerous.

That was the point I had spent months trying to make to him.

I stopped at the top of the hill and checked my weapon again.

My hands were shaking.

Love did not make me certain.

It made uncertainty matter more.

If Danse had known he was an Institute agent, I would have to face that. If his memories were false, I would have to face that too. If he hated me for refusing the execution order, I would survive it.

But I would not kill him because a category made the decision easier.

The bunker door waited below.

Before entering the code, I drew my weapon.

That hurt.

I did it anyway.

Love was not pretending risk did not exist.

Love was refusing to let fear become the only evidence admitted.

The lock accepted Haylen’s code.

Metal scraped open.

I stepped inside.

“Danse?”

My voice echoed down the corridor.

Nothing answered.

I tightened my grip on the weapon and headed for the elevator.

Whatever waited below, I would look at the person in front of me before the category.

I had asked Danse to learn that.

Now it was my turn.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
